rich_summary: Yudhishthira, believing fate cannot be avoided and bound by the king’s command and the warrior code, agrees to another game of dice despite knowing it will destroy him. The narrator compares this fatal lapse to Rama being deceived by the golden deer—an omen that minds cloud when calamity approaches. Sakuni proposes a final stake: the losing side must live twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year incognito, or repeat the exile if discovered. Ignoring warnings from those present, Yudhishthira accepts. Sakuni immediately declares victory, condemning the Pandavas to exile. As they discard their royal garments and don deer‑skins, Dussasana mocks them cruelly, boasting of Duryodhana’s triumph and humiliating Draupadi. This moment seals the Pandavas’ exile and intensifies the moral contrast between the two sides.

highlight_spans.why: Yudhishthira’s fatalistic reasoning about destiny and duty explains why he agrees to gamble despite foreseeing disaster.
The comparison to Rama being lured by the golden deer frames the moment as a classic sign of impending calamity clouding judgment.
Sakuni’s proposal of the exile wager establishes the pivotal condition that drives the next major arc of the epic.
Sakuni’s brief declaration of victory marks the decisive turning point sending the Pandavas into exile.
Dussasana’s taunting speech brutally humiliates the defeated Pandavas and Draupadi, intensifying the emotional and moral stakes.

top_scenes.scene_text: Yudhishthira and his brothers solemnly remove their royal robes in the court and clothe themselves in rough deer-skins as the assembly watches in grief and tension.
Sakuni casts the dice before the royal assembly, leaning forward with a sly smile as he declares, 'Lo, I have won,' while the Pandavas sit in stunned silence.
Dussasana stands gloating in the court, gesturing mockingly toward the newly exiled Pandavas and the humiliated Draupadi while courtiers react with shock and unease.
